text: Joab son of Zeruiah noticed that the king's heart had turned back toward Absalom.

So Joab sent to Tekoa for a wise woman and told her, "Please act like you're in mourning — put on mourning clothes, skip the oil, and behave like someone who has been grieving a dead person for a long time."
"Then go to the king and say what I tell you," and Joab fed her the exact words to use.
When the woman from Tekoa went in to the king, she dropped to the ground on her face, bowed low, and said, "Help me, my king!"
The king asked her, "What's wrong?" She answered, "I'm a widow — my husband has died."
"Your servant had two sons; they got into a fight out in the field with no one around to break it up, and one struck the other down and killed him."

"Now the whole family has turned against your servant, demanding I hand over the one who killed his brother so they can execute him for the life he took — even though that would wipe out the heir too. They'd snuff out the last coal I have left, leaving my husband no name or descendant on earth."
The king told the woman, "Go home; I will issue an order concerning you."
The woman of Tekoa said to the king, "My lord king, let any blame fall on me and my father's household — let the king and his throne be free of guilt."
The king replied, "If anyone gives you trouble over this, bring him to me and he won't bother you again."

She said, "Please, let the king invoke the name of the LORD your God, so the avenger of blood doesn't add to the destruction and wipe out my son." He said, "As surely as the LORD lives, not a single hair of your son's head will fall to the ground."
Then the woman said, "Please let your servant say one more thing to my lord the king." He said, "Go ahead."
She said, "Then why have you planned something similar against the people of God? By refusing to bring back his own exiled son, the king has, in effect, condemned himself with his own words."

"We're all going to die eventually — like water poured out on the ground that can't be scooped back up — but God doesn't simply take life away; he works out ways so that someone banished isn't kept cut off from him forever."
"The reason I've come to say this to my lord the king is that the people frightened me, and your servant thought, 'I'll speak to the king — maybe he'll grant his servant's request.'"
"Perhaps the king will listen and save his servant from the man trying to cut off both me and my son from what God gave us."
"Your servant thought, 'Let my lord the king's word set my mind at ease,' since my lord the king is like an angel of God at telling right from wrong. May the LORD your God be with you."
The king said to the woman, "Don't keep anything back from me that I ask you." She said, "Let my lord the king speak."

The king asked, "Is Joab's hand behind all of this?" The woman answered, "As surely as you live, my lord king, no one can dodge left or right from anything my lord the king says — yes, it was your servant Joab who told me what to do and put all these words in my mouth."
"Your servant Joab did this to turn the situation around, but my lord has wisdom like an angel of God, knowing everything that goes on in the land."
So the king told Joab, "Fine, I'll do it — go bring the young man Absalom back."
Joab dropped to the ground on his face, bowed low, and blessed the king, saying, "Today your servant knows he has your favor, my lord king, since the king has granted his servant's request."
Joab then got up, traveled to Geshur, and brought Absalom back to Jerusalem.
But the king ordered, "Let him go to his own house — he is not to see my face." So Absalom went to his own house and did not see the king.
Now there was no man in all Israel praised so highly for his good looks as Absalom — from the sole of his foot to the top of his head, he had no flaw at all.
Whenever he cut his hair — which he did once a year, since it grew too heavy to bear — he would weigh it, and it came to two hundred shekels by the royal standard.
Absalom had three sons and one daughter, whom he named Tamar; she grew up to be a beautiful woman.
Absalom lived in Jerusalem two full years without ever seeing the king's face.
Then Absalom sent word asking Joab to go speak to the king for him, but Joab wouldn't come; he sent for him a second time, and Joab still refused to come.
So he told his servants, "Look, Joab's field is right next to mine, and he's got barley growing there — go set it on fire." And Absalom's servants burned the field.
Joab then got up, came to Absalom's house, and demanded, "Why did your servants set my field on fire?"

Absalom told Joab, "Look, I sent for you and said, 'Come here so I can send you to ask the king why I ever bothered coming back from Geshur — I'd have been better off staying there.' Now let me see the king's face, and if I'm guilty of something, let him have me put to death."
So Joab went to the king and reported it; David sent for Absalom, who came in, bowed to the ground before the king, and the king kissed him.
